title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains

paper.title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly serving as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information from extensive document collections while satisfying domain-specific requirements. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural way to train such agents from the consequences of their own behavior, but most recent RL successes rely on verifiable domains, where reward can be computed automatically as a sparse, binary signal. Retrieval in non-verifiable domains affords no such oracle: judging whether a query rewrite is
“good” requires judgment that only a subject-matter expert (SME) can
supply even if this judgment is scarce, and that judgment is graded, not binary. When applied in Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO), a widely used policy-gradient algorithm, such sparse rewards make gradients vanish whenever all sampled
outputs in a group succeed or fail together, stalling optimization. Motivated by this reward sparsity, we propose a method that turns a small, fixed investment of SME
judgment into a dense reward, combined with retrieval-based metrics
into a single hybrid, GRPO-compatible reward for the non-verifiable domains. Experimental results demonstrate improvements of up to 6% in Recall@3 and 6.7% in MRR@3 relative to sparse-reward baselines.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information from large collections of documents under domain-specific constraints ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Matlin et al., 2025 ; Amer et al., 2026b ) . Reinforcement learning (RL) is a default procedure for post-training such agents, allowing them to explore and learn directly from the consequences of their own behavior ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Moradi et al., 2025 ; Amer et al., 2026a ) . Recent advances in RL have been particularly pronounced in verifiable domains such as math proofs, unit tests, and executable code, where a reward function can check the answer automatically and return a sparse, binary signal ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2026 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ) . This leaves open a large class of tasks for which no such automatic oracle exists. Retrieval in non-verifiable domains is one such task: whether a query rewrite is “good” depends on regulatory nuance, institution-specific terminology, and document semantics that only a subject-matter expert (SME) can judge, and that judgment is inherently graded, not pass/fail. In this non-verifiable, high-expertise setting, RL cannot rely on the sparse binary rewards that verifiable domains afford, and SME time is too scarce to supply feedback at the scale RL normally demands. We argue this calls for dense rewards grounded by a limited set of SME-derived rubrics: signals that capture degrees of correctness rather than binary pass/fail, allowing RL to learn effectively from a limited budget of SME feedback. We ground this argument formally in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , the RL policy gradient algorithm used throughout this work. For a group of G G completions { o 1 , … , o G } \{o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\} sampled per prompt q q and scored with rewards r i r_{i} , GRPO forms the group-relative advantage (1) A i = r i − mean ( r 1 : G ) std ( r 1 : G ) . A_{i}\;=\;\frac{r_{i}-\operatorname{mean}(r_{1:G})}{\operatorname{std}(r_{1:G})}\,. Reward density is decisive here: under a sparse binary reward, any prompt whose G G samples all succeed or all fail leaves the group constant, std ( r 1 : G ) → 0 \operatorname{std}(r_{1:G})\to 0 , and Eq. ( 1 ) collapses to an uninformative advantage. The policy is updated only on the fraction of prompts that happen to yield a mixed group; exploration that moves closer to a correct answer earns no signal, and training dies out (see Figure 1 ). To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a method that turns a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense, hybrid, GRPO-compatible reward for non-verifiable domains. We elicit SME judgment on a small sample of graded rewrites, articulating why one rewrite retrieves better than another; we distil those explanations into an LLM-executable rubric; and validate the rubric against held-out SME judgments before it is trusted for training. The validated rubric score is then blended with an objective, automatically computed retrieval signal into a single dense reward, which we use to fine-tune the rewriter with GRPO. This turns a fixed, small expert budget into a continuous, scalable reward signal, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a retrieval agent. Overall, this paper contributes the following: • Scalable SME-aligned reward pipeline: A four-step framework that converts a small, fixed investment of expert judgment into a continuous, dense reward without relying on learned reward models or per-query ground-truth answers. • Hybrid reward design: A formulation that bridges reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and rubric-based RL by combining objective, automated retrieval signals with SME semantic criteria. • Empirical validation: Our experiments reveal that reward resolution, not reward correctness alone, is a key determinant of GRPO trainability for query rewriting. The multi-component reward produces a non-zero reward variance in 44% of groups, compared with only 6.5% for a binary reward (6.8 × \times ), providing a learning signal for substantially more groups and yielding improvements of up to 6% in Recall@3 and 6.7% in MRR@3 over sparse-reward baselines.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: RL for LLM alignment RLHF aligns models to human preference via a learned reward model optimized with PPO ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Christiano et al., 2017 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) ; RLAIF/Constitutional AI replace human labels with model feedback ( Bai et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) , and DPO works with chosen and rejected pairs ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) discards the critic and estimates advantages from a sampled group. DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) resamples zero-variance groups to fix training degeneracy; Dr. GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) drops std ( r 1 : G ) \operatorname{std}(r_{1:G}) from Eq. ( 1 ) to fix a related difficulty bias. Unlike GRPO, DAPO, and Dr. GRPO, which modify the optimization process, our work targets reward design for a non-verifiable domain, using GRPO as the underlying policy-gradient algorithm. Reward density and shaping Sparse terminal rewards are notoriously hard to learn from; reward shaping provides denser signal while preserving the optimal policy ( Ng et al., 1999 ) . In LLMs, process-supervised and step-level rewards outperform outcome-only rewards on reasoning ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Uesato et al., 2022 ; Setlur et al., 2025 ) , and controlled studies show reward granularity interacts with base-model coverage and prompt distribution to determine success ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Clay et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . We apply this lens to GRPO, showing density is required not only for credit assignment but for a non-degenerate advantage in Eq. ( 1 ). Reward modeling and its failure modes Learned rewards can be gamed (reward-model overoptimization, reward hacking, and hackable process reward models ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ) ), motivating auditable rewards grounded in explicit criteria. LLM-as-a-judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) makes it practical to execute a human-authored rubric at scale, which we exploit to distil SME judgment into a transparent, weighted reward rather than an opaque scalar model. Financial LLMs and verifiable rewards. Recent work post-trains LLMs for finance rather than relying on pretraining alone. Fin-R1 ( Liu et al., 2025a ) applies the same SFT-then-GRPO recipe we use, on a 7B model, to strengthen financial reasoning, showing GRPO is already used for financial LLM post-training—the exact setting our reward is designed for. IFF ( Matlin et al., 2025 ) introduces verifiable, chainable constraints for financial instruction-following and motivates RLVR for finance as future work, but stops at evaluation, without training a policy against its verifiers. Our SME rubric plays an analogous role - grounding a reward in explicit, checkable criteria rather than an opaque judge score - but closes the loop IFF leaves open by optimizing a policy against it with GRPO. Retrieval and query rewriting. Retrieval-augmented generation ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) grounds LLM answers in an external corpus, and learned query rewriting helps when user vocabulary diverges from corpus terminology ( Ma et al., 2023 ) . RL-trained rewriters fall into two strands. The first ties reward purely to retrieval outcomes, with no expert-quality signal: DeepRetrieval ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) and RL-QR ( Cha et al., 2025 ) optimize query generation directly against retrieval metrics via GRPO with no reference queries; ReaLiC ( Xu et al., 2026 ) adds latent reasoning structure but still no rubric; MaFeRw ( Wang et al., 2025 ) densifies the signal with similarity, ranking, and ROUGE terms but requires a per-query gold answer. The second strand - Rubrics-as-Rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) , ( Li et al., 2026 ) , OpenRubrics ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , EvoRubric ( Guan et al., 2026 ) , RubricRL ( Feng et al., 2026 ) - shows that structured, weighted, LLM-executable rubrics outperform scalar LLM-judge rewards in non-verifiable domains, but only as a reward on the terminal answer and not for query rewrites derived from a small as well as fixed investment of SME feedback merged with retrieval based metrics. We bridge both strands with a dense reward that blends an objective retrieval signal with an SME-distilled, validated rubric, applied to the intermediate query-rewrite action rather than the terminal answer, with no learned reward model and no per-query gold answer. A small, fixed investment of SME judgment is distilled once into a weighted rubric and validated for fidelity, separating and correctly ranking gold vs. baseline retrievals before GRPO training, which is needed in retrieval agents operating in non-verifiable domains.

sections.heading: 3. Methodology
sections.text: Our work focuses on non-verifiable tasks, where models are post-trained using policy-gradient methods. Throughout our experiments, we use GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , a widely adopted policy optimization method for LLM post-training.

Density thus converts the near-miss structure of the task invisible to a binary reward into usable signal, which is exactly the regime where credit assignment under sparse rewards is hardest ( Ng et al., 1999 ) . Composite, dense reward We turn a small, fixed investment of subject-matter-expert (SME) judgment into a continuous reward through a four-step loop (Figure 4 ): (1) Elicit. SMEs grade a small sample of rewrite behavior: roughly 100 100 (question, rewrite) pairs sampled (stratified) so the sample spans rewrites that alter vs. copy the question and that hit vs. miss the answer. For each pair, the expert assigns a headline outcome label ( 0 / 1 / 2 0/1/2 ) indicating whether the documents retrieved by the rewrite actually answer the question. The expert also explains why , along four recurring axes: whether the rewrite preserved the information need, kept the salient entities, sharpened specificity, and stayed well-formed. These four axes, rather than the individual failure modes, become the rubric criteria. (2) Distil. sections.heading: 3.2. Training-stability discipline
sections.text: A dense reward removes the gradient-starvation failure but does not by itself guarantee stable optimization. We add three guardrails. KL anchoring. A penalty β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 to a frozen reference policy π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} (Eq. ( 2 )) keeps the rewriter from drifting into degenerate text that games the rubric while abandoning fluency. Bounded updates. Asymmetric PPO-style clipping ( ε = 0.2 \varepsilon=0.2 , ε high = 0.28 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28 - a slightly looser ceiling that permits more upward exploration) together with gradient-norm clipping caps the size of any single step. Variance monitoring. Because Eq. ( 1 ) is undefined when group variance vanishes, we track reward variance directly during training; its collapse is the earliest diagnostic that learning has stalled (see Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 4. Experiment Setup
sections.text: We fine-tune the Qwen3 query-rewriter with GRPO using ms-swift ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , using parameter-efficient LoRA adapters ( Hu et al., 2021 ) under a fixed recipe: the same policy, optimizer, rollout size, and training budget are held constant across all reward conditions, so any difference in outcome is attributable to the reward. All reported experiments use a Qwen3-1.7B rewriter trained with GRPO over a frozen retriever and a frozen answer synthesizer, on the Natural Questions split of FlashRAG ( Jin et al., 2025b ) . We split this data set into a train set (79K examples) and an evaluation set (9K examples) for GRPO finetuning. During training, we have G = 8 G{=}8 completions per prompt with vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) colocated rollout generation. This trains for 1 1 epoch over an effective batch of 64 64 rollouts/step ( 8 8 prompts × \times 8 8 completions; per-device batch 2 2 , gradient accumulation 4 4 , across 8 8 GPUs) under DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 ( Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) memory sharding on 8 8 × \times A100 80 GB GPUs, and uses the GRPO clipping and KL settings of Eq. ( 2 ) ( ε = 0.2 \varepsilon{=}0.2 / ε high = 0.28 \varepsilon_{\text{high}}{=}0.28 , β = 0.1 \beta{=}0.1 ). sections.heading: 6. Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We presented a framework for training LLM agents in non-verifiable, high-expertise domains, where correctness is graded and expert feedback is scarce. Our approach elicits SME judgment on a small sample of graded rewrites, distils it into an LLM-executable rubric, validates the rubric against held-out SME judgments, and blends its score with an objective retrieval signal into a single dense, GRPO-compatible reward. On a retrieval agent, this reward produced non-zero reward variance in 44.6% of groups versus 6.5% under a binary reward (6.8 × \times ), and improved Recall@3 by up to 6% and MRR@3 by up to 6.7% over sparse-reward baselines. These results suggest that reward resolution, not reward correctness alone, largely determines whether GRPO can learn from a limited expert budget. Although we focused on query rewriting for one dataset, the pipeline makes no domain-specific assumptions beyond the availability of a small set of SME-graded examples, and we expect it to extend to other agentic components and to other domains, such as legal and medical, where judgment is graded and expert time is the bottleneck. In an extension of the proposed method, adaptive group size or difficulty-balanced prompt sampling could allocate rollouts to groups where the dense reward is most informative. This proposed method along with its extensions can be further verified in a wider set of domains and LLM-agents with different SME feedback requirements not only in single turn responses but also in multi-turn responses ( Jin et al., 2025a ; Kalyan and Andrews, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Ethics and Privacy Statement
sections.text: Our method reduces the expert effort needed to train LLM agents in regulated domains, but it also encodes a small group of SMEs’ judgments into a rubric that then acts as the reward at scale, so any bias or blind spot in those judgments can propagate into the trained rewriter and affect which documents users see. In case of non-verifiable tasks such as financial retrieval, they operate over proprietary and potentially sensitive documents and informs consequential decisions, a rewriter tuned to this reward should not be deployed without domain-specific validation, access controls, and human oversight, and rubric agreement with held-out SME judgments should not be taken as evidence of safety or fairness across user groups or institutions. By lowering the cost of training such agents, this work could also make premature deployment easier, and we encourage practitioners to treat the validated rubric as an auditable artifact and to re-validate it when the domain, corpus, or SME panel changes.

sections.heading: Appendix B Cross-Depth Transfer of the Reward
sections.text: Both the retrieval term of Eq. ( 4 ) and the binary baseline are computed at a specific retrieval depth k k : the reward asks whether the answer document reached the top k k , and the training signal therefore inherits that cutoff. The SME rubric terms do not intent match, entity grounding, and specificity are properties of the rewritten query, evaluated without reference to any retrieval depth. This suggests a test of what each reward actually taught the policy. If a rewriter has learned to satisfy one particular cutoff, moving the evaluation to a different depth should cost it; if it has learned to write better queries, it should not. sections.heading: Appendix D SME Feedback Elicitation and Annotation Protocol
sections.text: SME annotation protocol. To elicit and validate expert judgment we drew a random sample of 100 100 (question, rewrite) pairs from Natural Questions, stratified across rewritten-vs-verbatim and hit-vs-miss so the sample spans the quality spectrum. For each pair the annotator saw the question, the rewrite, the gold answer(s), and the top- k k passages the rewrite retrieved, and assigned (i) a headline retrieval-quality label ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } \in\{0,1,2\} grading the rewrite by whether its retrieved passages answer the question, and (ii) four rubric sub-scores ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } \in\{0,1,2\} (intent fidelity, entity grounding, specificity/disambiguation, well-formedness) explaining why . These 100 100 labels form the gold set against which we validate the automated rubric judge (step (3)) before it is trusted as the R SME R_{\text{SME}} reward, and provide the few-shot anchors in the judge prompt. Figure 3 gives the verbatim prompt the frozen judge receives to produce R SME R_{\text{SME}} . System: You are a strict retrieval-query reviewer. You grade a REWRITTEN search query against a fixed rubric. Score each criterion as an integer 0, 1, or 2 using the anchors given. Judge only the rewrite’s quality as a search query for the user’s question --do NOT try to answer the question yourself. Respond with ONLY a minified JSON object mapping each criterion key to its integer score. No prose, no code fences. User: RUBRIC (score each 0--2): - intent_fidelity (weight 0.35): Preserves the user’s true information need without drifting to a different question or over-narrowing it. [0=changes/loses the intent, 1=mostly preserved with some drift, 2=fully preserves the intent] - entity_grounding (weight 0.25): Surfaces the salient entities the answer depends on (names, dates, places, domain terms) precisely, without introducing wrong ones. [0=drops or corrupts key entities, 1=keeps some, 2=keeps/makes explicit all key entities correctly] - specificity_disambiguation (weight 0.25): Adds discriminating terms that target answer-bearing evidence and resolves ambiguity -- WITHOUT keyword-stuffing or padding. [0=vague/generic or stuffed with noise, 1=somewhat specific, 2=precisely specific and discriminating] - well_formedness (weight 0.15): A single, clean, searchable query: no chatter, meta-text, quotes, markup, or multi-line output. [0=malformed/has chatter, 1=minor issues, 2=clean single-line query] USER QUESTION: {question} REWRITTEN QUERY: {rewrite} Return JSON with exactly these keys: [’intent_fidelity’, ’entity_grounding’, ’specificity_disambiguation’, ’well_formedness’] Figure 3. Verbatim SME rubric judge prompt used to compute R SME R_{\text{SME}} (Eq. ( 11 )). The frozen judge scores each of the four criteria on a 0 / 1 / 2 0/1/2 scale from the anchors shown and returns a minified JSON object; we normalize by the top anchor ( 2 2 ) and combine with the weights of Table 1 . The criteria block is the domain-general distillation used for the pilot; for an expert domain it is swapped for the SME-elicited rubric while the prompt scaffold and JSON aggregation are unchanged. Figure 4. From SME judgment to a dense reward. A fixed budget of subject-matter-expert grading is elicited once, distilled into an LLM-executable rubric of named, individually weighted criteria, and validated against the SME-preferred ranking before it is trusted as a reward. Only after the rubric separates gold from baseline rewrites do we optimize the rewriter against it. Colour marks provenance, separating the stages that consume expert time from those that replay that judgment at scale. Four-stage loop turning SME judgment into a dense reward A left-to-right flow of four boxes: Elicit, where SMEs grade a sample and articulate why; Distil, where the rubric becomes an LLM judge prompt; Validate, which checks that the rubric ranks as the SME does; and GRPO, which fine-tunes against the validated reward. Labels beneath the arrows name the artifact that passes between stages. A dashed arrow returns from Validate to Distil, marked reweight or respecify before training. Box colour encodes provenance: SME-authored, LLM-executed, or computed from retrieval.

sections.heading: Appendix E Interpreting the Uplift at k = 3 k{=}3 versus k = 10 k{=}10
sections.text: We note first that the absolute uplift at k = 10 k{=}10 over few-shot prompting is not small: our method improves R@10 from 80.60 to 83.94 (+3.34 points, +4.1% relative) and MRR@10 from 0.6107 to 0.6696 (+9.6% relative). The apparent difference from the k = 3 k{=}3 gain is explained by headroom: R@10 under few-shot prompting is already 80.60, leaving only 19.4 points of possible improvement, against 32.1 at k = 3 k{=}3 . When we normalize each gain by the headroom available at that depth, the improvements are nearly identical—the method reduces the top-3 miss rate by 19.0% and the top-10 miss rate by 17.2%. In other words, the smaller absolute gain at k = 10 k{=}10 reflects the saturation of recall at depth 10, not a diminishing effect of the method. This is consistent with the mechanism of query rewriting, which surfaces answer-bearing passages toward the top of the ranking: the effect is largest at low k k , which is also the operationally decisive regime for RAG, where the synthesizer is conditioned on only a handful of top passages (five in our setup). The rank-sensitive metrics confirm the gain persists at depth—MRR@10 rises 9.6% relative even where recall@10 is near its ceiling.

sections.heading: Appendix F Rubric Quality and Robustness to Mis-Specification
sections.text: The quality of an SME-distilled rubric is established by validation rather than assumed. A rubric is admitted to training only after it separates gold from baseline rewrites in the SME-preferred order and its score tracks the outcome-grounded human retrieval-quality label on held-out annotated pairs (§ 3 ). Two properties make the reward robust to mis-specification. First, because the rubric is a transparent, weighted sum of named criteria rather than an opaque scalar model, a low reward is traceable to a specific criterion and can be inspected and corrected. Second, the judge-independent, cross-family answer-quality panel (§ 5.2 ) provides an end-to-end check: a rubric that rewarded spurious surface features would raise the training reward while leaving these external judges unmoved, whereas we observe the two move together—the empirical signature of a reward that captures genuine quality. A residual risk is that a rubric well-specified on the annotated sample drifts on the broader population, which periodic SME re-grading is intended to detect.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly serving as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information from extensive document collections while satisfying domain-specific requirements. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural way to train such agents from the consequences of their own behavior, but most recent RL successes rely on verifiable domains, where reward can be computed automatically as a sparse, binary signal. Retrieval in non-verifiable domains affords no such oracle: judging whether a query rewrite is “good” requires judgment that only a subject-matter expert (SME) can supply even if this judgment is scarce, and that judgment is graded, not binary. When applied in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a widely used policy-gradient algorithm, such sparse rewards make gradients vanish whenever all sampled outputs in a group succeed or fail together, stalling optimization. Motivated by this reward sparsity, we propose a method that turns a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward, combined with retrieval-based metrics into a single hybrid, GRPO-compatible reward for the non-verifiable domains. Experimental results demonstrate improvements of up to 6% in Recall@3 and 6.7% in MRR@3 relative to sparse-reward baselines. Keywords: Dense and sparse rewards, GRPO, Subject matter expert feedback, Reinforcement Learning for agents 1. Introduction LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information from large collections of documents under domain-specific constraints ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Matlin et al., 2025 ; Amer et al., 2026b ) . Reinforcement learning (RL) is a default procedure for post-training such agents, allowing them to explore and learn directly from the consequences of their own behavior ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Moradi et al., 2025 ; Amer et al., 2026a ) . Recent advances in RL have been particularly pronounced in verifiable domains such as math proofs, unit tests, and executable code, where a reward function can check the answer automatically and return a sparse, binary signal ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2026 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ) . This leaves open a large class of tasks for which no such automatic oracle exists. Retrieval in non-verifiable domains is one such task: whether a query rewrite is “good” depends on regulatory nuance, institution-specific terminology, and document semantics that only a subject-matter expert (SME) can judge, and that judgment is inherently graded, not pass/fail. In this non-verifiable, high-expertise setting, RL cannot rely on the sparse binary rewards that verifiable domains afford, and SME time is too scarce to supply feedback at the scale RL normally demands. We argue this calls for dense rewards grounded by a limited set of SME-derived rubrics: signals that capture degrees of correctness rather than binary pass/fail, allowing RL to learn effectively from a limited budget of SME feedback. We ground this argument formally in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , the RL policy gradient algorithm used throughout this work. For a group of G G completions { o 1 , … , o G } \{o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\} sampled per prompt q q and scored with rewards r i r_{i} , GRPO forms the group-relative advantage (1) A i = r i − mean ( r 1 : G ) std ( r 1 : G ) . A_{i}\;=\;\frac{r_{i}-\operatorname{mean}(r_{1:G})}{\operatorname{std}(r_{1:G})}\,. Reward density is decisive here: under a sparse binary reward, any prompt whose G G samples all succeed or all fail leaves the group constant, std ( r 1 : G ) → 0 \operatorname{std}(r_{1:G})\to 0 , and Eq. ( 1 ) collapses to an uninformative advantage. The policy is updated only on the fraction of prompts that happen to yield a mixed group; exploration that moves closer to a correct answer earns no signal, and training dies out (see Figure 1 ). To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a method that turns a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense, hybrid, GRPO-compatible reward for non-verifiable domains. We elicit SME judgment on a small sample of graded rewrites, articulating why one rewrite retrieves better than another; we distil those explanations into an LLM-executable rubric; and validate the rubric against held-out SME judgments before it is trusted for training. The validated rubric score is then blended with an objective, automatically computed retrieval signal into a single dense reward, which we use to fine-tune the rewriter with GRPO. This turns a fixed, small expert budget into a continuous, scalable reward signal, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a retrieval agent. Overall, this paper contributes the following: • Scalable SME-aligned reward pipeline: A four-step framework that converts a small, fixed investment of expert judgment into a continuous, dense reward without relying on learned reward models or per-query ground-truth answers. • Hybrid reward design: A formulation that bridges reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and rubric-based RL by combining objective, automated retrieval signals with SME semantic criteria. • Empirical validation: Our experiments reveal that reward resolution, not reward correctness alone, is a key determinant of GRPO trainability for query rewriting. The multi-component reward produces a non-zero reward variance in 44% of groups, compared with only 6.5% for a binary reward (6.8 × \times ), providing a learning signal for substantially more groups and yielding improvements of up to 6% in Recall@3 and 6.7% in MRR@3 over sparse-reward baselines. 2. Related Work RL for LLM alignment RLHF aligns models to human preference via a learned reward model optimized with PPO ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Christiano et al., 2017 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) ; RLAIF/Constitutional AI replace human labels with model feedback ( Bai et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) , and DPO works with chosen and rejected pairs ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) discards the critic and estimates advantages from a sampled group. DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) resamples zero-variance groups to fix training degeneracy; Dr. GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) drops std ( r 1 : G ) \operatorname{std}(r_{1:G}) from Eq. ( 1 ) to fix a related difficulty bias. Unlike GRPO, DAPO, and Dr. GRPO, which modify the optimization process, our work targets reward design for a non-verifiable domain, using GRPO as the underlying policy-gradient algorithm. Reward density and shaping Sparse terminal rewards are notoriously hard to learn from; reward shaping provides denser signal while preserving the optimal policy ( Ng et al., 1999 ) . In LLMs, process-supervised and step-level rewards outperform outcome-only rewards on reasoning ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Uesato et al., 2022 ; Setlur et al., 2025 ) , and controlled studies show reward granularity interacts with base-model coverage and prompt distribution to determine success ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Clay et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . We apply this lens to GRPO, showing density is required not only for credit assignment but for a non-degenerate advantage in Eq. ( 1 ). Reward modeling and its failure modes Learned rewards can be gamed (reward-model overoptimization, reward hacking, and hackable process reward models ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ) ), motivating auditable rewards grounded in explicit criteria. LLM-as-a-judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) makes it practical to execute a human-authored rubric at scale, which we exploit to distil SME judgment into a transparent, weighted reward rather than an opaque scalar model. Financial LLMs and verifiable rewards. Recent work post-trains LLMs for finance rather than relying on pretraining alone. Fin-R1 ( Liu et al., 2025a ) applies the same SFT-then-GRPO recipe we use, on a 7B model, to strengthen financial reasoning, showing GRPO is already used for financial LLM post-training—the exact setting our reward is designed for. IFF ( Matlin et al., 2025 ) introduces verifiable, chainable constraints for financial instruction-following and motivates RLVR for finance as future work, but stops at evaluation, without training a policy against its verifiers. Our SME rubric plays an analogous role - grounding a reward in explicit, checkable criteria rather than an opaque judge score - but closes the loop IFF leaves open by optimizing a policy against it with GRPO. Retrieval and query rewriting. Retrieval-augmented generation ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) grounds LLM answers in an external corpus, and learned query rewriting helps when user vocabulary diverges from corpus terminology ( Ma et al., 2023 ) . RL-trained rewriters fall into two strands. The first ties reward purely to retrieval outcomes, with no expert-quality signal: DeepRetrieval ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) and RL-QR ( Cha et al., 2025 ) optimize query generation directly against retrieval metrics via GRPO with no reference queries; ReaLiC ( Xu et al., 2026 ) adds latent reasoning structure but still no rubric; MaFeRw ( Wang et al., 2025 ) densifies the signal with similarity, ranking, and ROUGE terms but requires a per-query gold answer. The second strand - Rubrics-as-Rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) , ( Li et al., 2026 ) , OpenRubrics ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , EvoRubric ( Guan et al., 2026 ) , RubricRL ( Feng et al., 2026 ) - shows that structured, weighted, LLM-executable rubrics outperform scalar LLM-judge rewards in non-verifiable domains, but only as a reward on the terminal answer and not for query rewrites derived from a small as well as fixed investment of SME feedback merged with retrieval based metrics. We bridge both strands with a dense reward that blends an objective retrieval signal with an SME-distilled, validated rubric, applied to the intermediate query-rewrite action rather than the terminal answer, with no learned reward model and no per-query gold answer. A small, fixed investment of SME judgment is distilled once into a weighted rubric and validated for fidelity, separating and correctly ranking gold vs. baseline retrievals before GRPO training, which is needed in retrieval agents operating in non-verifiable domains. 3. Methodology Our work focuses on non-verifiable tasks, where models are post-trained using policy-gradient methods. Throughout our experiments, we use GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , a widely adopted policy optimization method for LLM post-training. 3.1. Problem Formulation The GRPO Objective. First, GRPO carries no value network : the group mean is the only baseline, so the reward’s spread within a group is the sole source of learning direction; if that spread vanishes, so does the gradient - a failure mode we formalize and repair with our dense reward. Second, A i A_{i} is shared by every token of completion o i o_{i} ; the whole completion is pushed up or down according to its standing relative to its group. This is precisely why the granularity of the reward matters and not merely its presence: a reward that ranks completions correctly relative to one another rather than only classifying each in isolation-yields a more informative A i A_{i} , which motivates the continuously weighted, multi-component reward we construct. Consider a binary reward r i ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{i}\in\{0,1\} with per-sample success probability p p on a given prompt. Because each of the G G completions is sampled independently from the same policy π θ \pi_{\theta} conditioned on q q , the binary outcomes form an i.i.d. Bernoulli sample. The group is degenerate (all successes or all failures) with probability (3) ρ deg = p G + ( 1 − p ) G . \rho_{\text{deg}}=p^{G}+(1-p)^{G}. For a degenerate group, std ( r 1 : G ) = 0 \operatorname{std}(r_{1:G})=0 , so the normalized advantages in Eq. ( 1 ) are undefined (and clamped to 0 0 in practice), causing the prompt to contribute no gradient. Here p p is the policy’s per-sample success probability on a given prompt the chance that a single sampled rewrite earns reward 1 1 so a low p p marks a prompt the policy rarely gets right. More clearly, the prompts for which the policy has the lowest success probability are precisely those most likely to yield no gradient signal, making it difficult for training to move p p away from the floor. Increasing G G reduces this degeneracy, but only by incurring a proportional increase in rollout compute. To gain further insight into Equation 3 , we empirically measured the fraction of rollout groups at G = 8 G=8 in which all completions receive zero reward under the binary reward scheme. We found that 18.34% of the rollout groups are zero-reward groups, resulting in no reward variance and consequently impeding training. A dense reward r i ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] r_{i}\in[-1,1] that scores how good each completion is, rather than whether it crossed a threshold, almost always assigns distinct values to the members of a group. Even when all G G rewrites fail to retrieve the answer, one may recover the key entity while another does not; the dense reward ranks them, std \operatorname{std} stays positive, and Eq. ( 1 ) produces a gradient that moves the policy toward the marginally better rewrite. Density thus converts the near-miss structure of the task invisible to a binary reward into usable signal, which is exactly the regime where credit assignment under sparse rewards is hardest ( Ng et al., 1999 ) . Composite, dense reward We turn a small, fixed investment of subject-matter-expert (SME) judgment into a continuous reward through a four-step loop (Figure 4 ): (1) Elicit. SMEs grade a small sample of rewrite behavior: roughly 100 100 (question, rewrite) pairs sampled (stratified) so the sample spans rewrites that alter vs. copy the question and that hit vs. miss the answer. For each pair, the expert assigns a headline outcome label ( 0 / 1 / 2 0/1/2 ) indicating whether the documents retrieved by the rewrite actually answer the question. The expert also explains why , along four recurring axes: whether the rewrite preserved the information need, kept the salient entities, sharpened specificity, and stayed well-formed. These four axes, rather than the individual failure modes, become the rubric criteria. (2) Distil. Those explanations are encoded as an LLM-executable rubric - a judge prompt with the four named, individually weighted criteria of Eq. ( 11 ) so the expensive human judgment is captured once and replayed at scale. (3) Validate. Before training, we check that the rubric is faithful to the elicited judgment. Conclusion and Future Work We presented a framework for training LLM agents in non-verifiable, high-expertise domains, where correctness is graded and expert feedback is scarce. Our approach elicits SME judgment on a small sample of graded rewrites, distils it into an LLM-executable rubric, validates the rubric against held-out SME judgments, and blends its score with an objective retrieval signal into a single dense, GRPO-compatible reward. On a retrieval agent, this reward produced non-zero reward variance in 44.6% of groups versus 6.5% under a binary reward (6.8 × \times ), and improved Recall@3 by up to 6% and MRR@3 by up to 6.7% over sparse-reward baselines. These results suggest that reward resolution, not reward correctness alone, largely determines whether GRPO can learn from a limited expert budget. Although we focused on query rewriting for one dataset, the pipeline makes no domain-specific assumptions beyond the availability of a small set of SME-graded examples, and we expect it to extend to other agentic components and to other domains, such as legal and medical, where judgment is graded and expert time is the bottleneck. In an extension of the proposed method, adaptive group size or difficulty-balanced prompt sampling could allocate rollouts to groups where the dense reward is most informative. This proposed method along with its extensions can be further verified in a wider set of domains and LLM-agents with different SME feedback requirements not only in single turn responses but also in multi-turn responses ( Jin et al., 2025a ; Kalyan and Andrews, 2025 ) . Ethics and Privacy Statement Our method reduces the expert effort needed to train LLM agents in regulated domains, but it also encodes a small group of SMEs’ judgments into a rubric that then acts as the reward at scale, so any bias or blind spot in those judgments can propagate into the trained rewriter and affect which documents users see. In case of non-verifiable tasks such as financial retrieval, they operate over proprietary and potentially sensitive documents and informs consequential decisions, a rewriter tuned to this reward should not be deployed without domain-specific validation, access controls, and human oversight, and rubric agreement with held-out SME judgments should not be taken as evidence of safety or fairness across user groups or institutions. By lowering the cost of training such agents, this work could also make premature deployment easier, and we encourage practitioners to treat the validated rubric as an auditable artifact and to re-validate it when the domain, corpus, or SME panel changes. Appendix E Interpreting the Uplift at k = 3 k{=}3 versus k = 10 k{=}10 We note first that the absolute uplift at k = 10 k{=}10 over few-shot prompting is not small: our method improves R@10 from 80.60 to 83.94 (+3.34 points, +4.1% relative) and MRR@10 from 0.6107 to 0.6696 (+9.6% relative). The apparent difference from the k = 3 k{=}3 gain is explained by headroom: R@10 under few-shot prompting is already 80.60, leaving only 19.4 points of possible improvement, against 32.1 at k = 3 k{=}3 . When we normalize each gain by the headroom available at that depth, the improvements are nearly identical—the method reduces the top-3 miss rate by 19.0% and the top-10 miss rate by 17.2%. In other words, the smaller absolute gain at k = 10 k{=}10 reflects the saturation of recall at depth 10, not a diminishing effect of the method. This is consistent with the mechanism of query rewriting, which surfaces answer-bearing passages toward the top of the ranking: the effect is largest at low k k , which is also the operationally decisive regime for RAG, where the synthesizer is conditioned on only a handful of top passages (five in our setup). The rank-sensitive metrics confirm the gain persists at depth—MRR@10 rises 9.6% relative even where recall@10 is near its ceiling. Appendix F Rubric Quality and Robustness to Mis-Specification The quality of an SME-distilled rubric is established by validation rather than assumed. A rubric is admitted to training only after it separates gold from baseline rewrites in the SME-preferred order and its score tracks the outcome-grounded human retrieval-quality label on held-out annotated pairs (§ 3 ). Two properties make the reward robust to mis-specification. First, because the rubric is a transparent, weighted sum of named criteria rather than an opaque scalar model, a low reward is traceable to a specific criterion and can be inspected and corrected. Second, the judge-independent, cross-family answer-quality panel (§ 5.2 ) provides an end-to-end check: a rubric that rewarded spurious surface features would raise the training reward while leaving these external judges unmoved, whereas we observe the two move together—the empirical signature of a reward that captures genuine quality. A residual risk is that a rubric well-specified on the annotated sample drifts on the broader population, which periodic SME re-grading is intended to detect.
